name: Porter's Five Forces
extended_summary: Michael Porter's framework analyzes industry profitability through five competitive forces that collectively determine the intensity of competition and ultimate profit potential. Threat of new entrants, bargaining power of buyers, bargaining power of suppliers, threat of substitutes, and rivalry among existing competitors interact to set the structural ceiling on industry returns. The framework was a foundational contribution to strategic management and remains widely taught despite criticisms about its static nature and focus on industry rather than firm-specific capabilities.
core_components: Threat of new entrants; Bargaining power of buyers; Bargaining power of suppliers; Threat of substitute products; Competitive rivalry
primary_use_case: Industry attractiveness analysis and competitive positioning during strategic planning.
common_criticisms: Static rather than dynamic; underweights complementary products and ecosystem effects; focuses on industry structure over firm capabilities; assumes clear industry boundaries that often blur in practice.
primary_sources: Porter, M.E. (1979). 'How Competitive Forces Shape Strategy', Harvard Business Review; Porter, M.E. (1980). Competitive Strategy
siblings: Porter's Generic Strategies; Porter's Value Chain; SWOT Analysis; PESTLE Analysis

name: OKRs
extended_summary: Objectives and Key Results is a goal-setting framework pairing ambitious qualitative objectives with measurable quantitative key results that indicate progress. Originated at Intel under Andy Grove as a refinement of MBO, then introduced to Google by John Doerr where it became the canonical implementation. OKRs are typically set quarterly, scored on a 0.0-1.0 scale at quarter end, and explicitly designed to encourage stretch goals such that 0.7 represents successful achievement.
core_components: Objective (qualitative direction); Key Results (typically 3-5 measurable outcomes); Cadence (typically quarterly); Scoring (0.0-1.0); Stretch ambition
primary_use_case: Aligning organizational, team, and individual goals around measurable outcomes with quarterly cadence.
common_criticisms: Often degenerates into KPI tracking when stretch ambition is dropped; cascading from top-down can become bureaucratic; requires cultural fit with high-trust environments; quarterly cadence may not match natural work rhythms in all domains.
primary_sources: Grove, A. (1983). High Output Management; Doerr, J. (2018). Measure What Matters
siblings: Balanced Scorecard; Hoshin Kanri; Management by Objectives

name: Big Five
extended_summary: The Five-Factor Model of personality identifies five broad dimensions (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Neuroticism) that have replicated across decades of factor-analytic research and across cultures. The model emerged from lexical analysis of personality descriptors in natural language and was consolidated through the work of Costa and McCrae and others in the 1980s and 1990s. It is the dominant taxonomy in academic personality psychology and shows modest predictive validity for life outcomes including job performance, relationship stability, and longevity.
originators: Lewis Goldberg; Paul Costa; Robert McCrae (consolidation); Ernest Tupes and Raymond Christal (early factor work)
core_components: Openness to experience; Conscientiousness; Extraversion; Agreeableness; Neuroticism (also called Emotional Stability when reverse-scored)
primary_use_case: Academic personality research; industrial-organizational assessment; clinical and counseling applications.
common_criticisms: Five factors may collapse meaningful variation captured by more granular models like HEXACO; descriptive rather than explanatory (doesn't tell you why traits cluster); Western cultural origin may limit cross-cultural applicability despite replication studies.
primary_sources: Costa, P.T. & McCrae, R.R. (1992). NEO Personality Inventory manual; Goldberg, L.R. (1990). 'An alternative description of personality: The Big Five factor structure'
siblings: HEXACO; Hogan Personality Inventory; Myers-Briggs Type Indicator; Enneagram

name: REST
extended_summary: Representational State Transfer is an architectural style for distributed hypermedia systems defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 doctoral dissertation. REST imposes constraints (statelessness, uniform interface, client-server separation, layered system, cacheability, code-on-demand) that yield desirable properties for web-scale systems including scalability and evolvability. The style was derived by analyzing what made the early web successful and is now the dominant architectural pattern for web APIs, though most APIs called 'REST' violate one or more of Fielding's original constraints.
core_components: Statelessness; Uniform interface (resources, representations, self-descriptive messages, HATEOAS); Client-server separation; Layered system; Cacheability; Code-on-demand (optional)
primary_use_case: Designing web APIs and distributed hypermedia systems intended to scale across the open internet.
common_criticisms: Most 'REST' APIs are not actually RESTful (HATEOAS is widely ignored); HTTP semantics are often misused; less efficient than RPC for high-throughput service-to-service calls; doesn't naturally fit real-time or streaming use cases.
primary_sources: Fielding, R.T. (2000). Architectural Styles and the Design of Network-based Software Architectures (PhD dissertation, UC Irvine)
siblings: SOAP; GraphQL; gRPC; Hexagonal Architecture

name: OODA Loop
extended_summary: John Boyd's decision cycle of Observe, Orient, Decide, Act describes how an agent processes information and acts in adversarial contexts. The framework's central claim is that operating inside an opponent's OODA loop — cycling faster while remaining accurate — produces decisive advantage by inducing confusion and paralysis. Boyd developed the framework during fighter pilot work in the 1950s-60s and progressively expanded it into a general theory of conflict applicable to military strategy, business competition, and individual decision-making.
core_components: Observe; Orient (the most weighted phase, encompassing cultural heritage, genetic heritage, prior experience, analysis/synthesis, new information); Decide; Act; Implicit guidance and control loops
primary_use_case: Adversarial decision-making in military operations, business competition, and any context requiring fast adaptive response.
common_criticisms: The 'faster loop wins' summary oversimplifies Boyd's emphasis on Orientation as the critical phase; popularized as a catchy diagram that misses the framework's depth; difficult to operationalize the Orient phase rigorously.
primary_sources: Boyd, J. (presentations 1970s-1990s, never formally published); Coram, R. (2002). Boyd: The Fighter Pilot Who Changed the Art of War; Osinga, F. (2007). Science, Strategy and War
siblings: Maneuver Warfare; Mission Command; Cynefin Framework

name: Myers-Briggs Type Indicator
extended_summary: The MBTI is a personality typology classifying individuals into one of sixteen types from four dichotomies (Extraversion/Introversion, Sensing/Intuition, Thinking/Feeling, Judging/Perceiving). Developed by Isabel Briggs Myers and her mother Katharine Cook Briggs from Carl Jung's typological theory, it became enormously popular in corporate training and team-building contexts. Mainstream personality psychology rejects it on psychometric grounds — its forced-choice dichotomies impose categorical structure on continuously distributed traits, test-retest reliability is poor, and predictive validity beyond chance has not been established.
originators: Isabel Briggs Myers; Katharine Cook Briggs
core_components: Extraversion/Introversion; Sensing/Intuition; Thinking/Feeling; Judging/Perceiving; sixteen resulting types
primary_use_case: Corporate team-building, career counseling, and self-development contexts; use in high-stakes decisions like hiring is generally discouraged by mainstream psychology.
common_criticisms: Forced-choice dichotomies misrepresent continuous trait distributions; weak test-retest reliability with many people changing types on retest; lack of empirical validation for the sixteen-type structure; rejected by mainstream personality psychology in favor of dimensional models like the Big Five.
primary_sources: Myers, I.B. & Briggs, K. (1962). Myers-Briggs Type Indicator manual; Jung, C.G. (1921). Psychological Types (theoretical foundation)
siblings: Big Five; HEXACO; DISC Assessment; Enneagram

name: Polyvagal Theory
extended_summary: Stephen Porges' theory proposes three vagal pathways governing autonomic responses to safety, threat mobilization, and shutdown — with the ventral vagal complex enabling social engagement, the sympathetic system mediating fight/flight, and the dorsal vagal complex producing immobilization. The theory has been widely adopted in trauma therapy, where its language of nervous system states has provided practitioners with useful clinical scaffolding. The underlying neurophysiology, particularly the claim about a phylogenetically distinct mammalian ventral vagal pathway and its role in social engagement, has been seriously challenged by mainstream physiologists who argue Porges' specific anatomical and evolutionary claims do not match the evidence.
core_components: Ventral vagal complex (social engagement); Sympathetic activation (mobilization); Dorsal vagal complex (immobilization); Neuroception (subconscious threat detection); Hierarchical response sequence
primary_use_case: Trauma-informed therapy, somatic experiencing, and clinical work centered on autonomic nervous system regulation.
common_criticisms: Specific neuroanatomical and evolutionary claims have been challenged by mainstream physiology (Grossman and others); the theory's wide therapeutic adoption outpaces its empirical validation; some clinical claims appear to be metaphorically rather than literally true.
primary_sources: Porges, S.W. (1995). 'Orienting in a defensive world: Mammalian modifications of our evolutionary heritage', Psychophysiology; Porges, S.W. (2011). The Polyvagal Theory
siblings: Attachment Theory; Trauma-Informed Care; Internal Family Systems

name: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
extended_summary: Abraham Maslow's framework arranges human needs into a hierarchy from physiological needs through safety, belonging, esteem, and self-actualization, with self-transcendence added in his later work. The framework proposes that lower needs must be substantially met before higher needs become motivating, producing the iconic pyramid representation that Maslow himself never drew. Empirical research has not supported the strict hierarchy — people pursue multiple needs simultaneously, and the ordering is not universal — though the underlying needs categories remain useful as a checklist of motivational dimensions.
core_components: Physiological needs; Safety needs; Love and belonging; Esteem; Self-actualization; Self-transcendence (added later)
primary_use_case: Introductory psychology and management training; rough motivational diagnostics; humanistic-psychology-informed practice.
common_criticisms: Strict hierarchical ordering not empirically supported; pyramid representation was added by others, not Maslow; methodologically weak original sources (biographical analysis of select individuals); limited cross-cultural validation; needs categories can be useful even when the hierarchy is rejected.
primary_sources: Maslow, A. (1943). 'A Theory of Human Motivation', Psychological Review; Maslow, A. (1954). Motivation and Personality
siblings: Self-Determination Theory; Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory; PERMA

name: Spotify Model
extended_summary: An organizational pattern for scaling agile teams using cross-functional 'squads' grouped into 'tribes', with 'chapters' connecting people of the same discipline across squads and 'guilds' as voluntary communities of interest. Documented by Henrik Kniberg and Anders Ivarsson around 2012 based on Spotify's organizational structure at the time, the model became enormously popular as a template for scaling agile in technology organizations. Spotify itself has acknowledged that the model wasn't fully accurate even when documented and that the company has substantially evolved away from it; nonetheless the terminology persists in agile transformation contexts.
core_components: Squads (cross-functional autonomous teams); Tribes (collections of related squads); Chapters (discipline-aligned groups within tribes); Guilds (cross-organizational communities of interest)
primary_use_case: Reference template for scaling agile in technology organizations; often used in agile transformation initiatives.
common_criticisms: Was an aspirational snapshot, not a steady-state description, even when documented; Spotify itself moved away from key elements; widely cargo-culted without understanding the cultural prerequisites; treats organizational design as transferable when it depends on specific context.
primary_sources: Kniberg, H. & Ivarsson, A. (2012). 'Scaling Agile @ Spotify' (whitepaper)
siblings: Scrum; SAFe; LeSS; Holacracy

name: Capital Asset Pricing Model
extended_summary: CAPM relates the expected return of an asset to its systematic risk via the equation E(R) = Rf + β(E(Rm) - Rf), where beta measures the asset's covariance with the market portfolio. Developed independently by William Sharpe, John Lintner, and Jan Mossin in the early-to-mid 1960s building on Markowitz's portfolio theory, the model provides a theoretical foundation for risk-adjusted pricing. Empirical performance has been substantially challenged — Fama and French's three-factor and five-factor extensions emerged precisely because CAPM beta alone explains less of cross-sectional return variation than the model predicts — but it remains foundational in finance education and the source of widely-used concepts like systematic versus idiosyncratic risk.
originators: William Sharpe; John Lintner; Jan Mossin (independent developments)
core_components: Risk-free rate; Market risk premium; Beta (sensitivity to market returns); Security market line; Assumption of efficient markets and homogeneous expectations
primary_use_case: Estimating cost of equity for valuation; risk-adjusted performance measurement; academic finance teaching foundation.
common_criticisms: Empirical predictions weak — beta alone explains less cross-sectional variation than predicted; assumptions (efficient markets, homogeneous expectations, single-period horizon) are unrealistic; superseded for many applications by Fama-French multifactor models.
primary_sources: Sharpe, W.F. (1964). 'Capital Asset Prices: A Theory of Market Equilibrium under Conditions of Risk', Journal of Finance; Lintner, J. (1965). 'The Valuation of Risk Assets...'
siblings: Modern Portfolio Theory; Efficient Market Hypothesis; Fama-French models

name: Bourdieu's Habitus
extended_summary: Pierre Bourdieu's framework treats social practice as the product of three interlocking concepts: habitus (durable embodied dispositions acquired through socialization), field (a structured social space with its own logic and stakes), and capital (resources of various forms — economic, cultural, social, symbolic — that confer position and power within fields). Practice emerges from the interaction of habitus and field, with capital determining one's effective position. The framework's power lies in dissolving the dichotomy between structural determinism and individual agency by treating dispositions as both structured by past experience and structuring of future action.
core_components: Habitus (embodied dispositions); Field (structured social space); Capital (economic, cultural, social, symbolic forms); Practice (the outcome); Doxa (taken-for-granted assumptions of a field); Symbolic violence
primary_use_case: Sociological analysis of how social structures reproduce themselves through individual action; cultural studies; analysis of class, taste, education, and professional fields.
common_criticisms: Habitus has been criticized as overly deterministic despite Bourdieu's intentions; concepts can become reified rather than analytical; difficult to operationalize for empirical research; thick prose style limits accessibility.
primary_sources: Bourdieu, P. (1977). Outline of a Theory of Practice; Bourdieu, P. (1984). Distinction; Bourdieu, P. (1990). The Logic of Practice
siblings: Structuration Theory; Practice Theory; Foucault's Power-Knowledge

name: Liminality
extended_summary: Originally developed by Arnold van Gennep in his 1909 work on rites of passage and substantially extended by Victor Turner in the 1960s and 70s, liminality describes the threshold state in which participants in a transition have left their previous identity but not yet assumed a new one. Turner emphasized the structural ambiguity of the liminal phase, the suspension of ordinary social hierarchies, and the emergence of communitas — an unstructured equality among those undergoing transition together. The concept has expanded beyond ritual studies into organizational change, identity development, and analyses of disruption.
core_components: Separation phase; Liminal/threshold phase; Reaggregation phase; Communitas (unstructured solidarity in liminality); Anti-structure; Liminoid (Turner's extension to non-ritual contexts)
primary_use_case: Anthropological analysis of ritual and transition; studies of organizational change; identity development theory; analyses of crisis and disruption.
common_criticisms: Western framing may not generalize to all cultural contexts; over-extension to any transitional state risks emptying the concept; communitas may be idealized; structure/anti-structure distinction may be too binary.
primary_sources: van Gennep, A. (1909). The Rites of Passage; Turner, V. (1969). The Ritual Process; Turner, V. (1974). Dramas, Fields, and Metaphors
siblings: Rites of Passage; Hero's Journey; Bridges' Transition Model

name: Generative Grammar
extended_summary: Noam Chomsky's framework treats grammar as a finite system of formal rules capable of generating the infinite set of grammatical sentences in a language. The framework launched modern theoretical linguistics by reframing the central question from describing surface patterns to characterizing the underlying competence that produces them. Generative grammar has gone through several distinct theoretical phases — Standard Theory, Government and Binding, Minimalism — each refining the formal apparatus, with the Minimalist Program being Chomsky's current articulation. Specific universal-grammar claims about innate linguistic structure have been increasingly contested by usage-based and constructionist alternatives.
core_components: Competence vs performance; Deep structure vs surface structure (in earlier phases); Universal Grammar; Phrase structure rules; Transformations (in earlier phases); Minimalist Program (current)
primary_use_case: Theoretical linguistics; formal characterization of natural language syntax; cognitive science accounts of language acquisition.
common_criticisms: Specific Universal Grammar claims contested by usage-based and constructionist linguists; theory has gone through multiple major revisions which raises Lakatosian questions about its protective belt; emphasis on competence over performance leaves much linguistic data outside scope; cross-linguistic typology has revealed more variation than UG predicts.
primary_sources: Chomsky, N. (1957). Syntactic Structures; Chomsky, N. (1965). Aspects of the Theory of Syntax; Chomsky, N. (1995). The Minimalist Program
siblings: Universal Grammar; Construction Grammar; Functional Grammar; Optimality Theory

name: Niche Construction
extended_summary: An evolutionary framework arguing that organisms actively modify their own and others' environments, with these modifications altering selection pressures in ways that feed back into evolutionary trajectories. Beavers building dams, earthworms processing soil, and humans building cities all create what the framework's proponents call ecological inheritance — environmental modifications that persist across generations alongside genetic inheritance. The framework challenges the standard view of organisms as passive recipients of selection pressures and has gained traction within the broader Extended Evolutionary Synthesis movement, though it remains contested within mainstream evolutionary biology about how much explanatory weight ecological inheritance deserves.
originators: F. John Odling-Smee; Kevin Laland; Marcus Feldman
core_components: Genetic inheritance; Ecological inheritance; Niche construction (active environmental modification); Feedback to selection pressures; Coupling of evolutionary and ecological dynamics
primary_use_case: Evolutionary theory; ecology; cultural evolution; debates about the Extended Evolutionary Synthesis.
common_criticisms: Disputed within mainstream evolutionary biology about whether it adds explanatory power beyond standard selection; the boundary between ordinary phenotypic effects and 'true' niche construction is contested; risk of reifying a phenomenon that is already implicit in standard accounts.
primary_sources: Odling-Smee, F.J., Laland, K.N. & Feldman, M.W. (2003). Niche Construction: The Neglected Process in Evolution
siblings: Modern Synthesis; Punctuated Equilibrium; Selfish Gene Theory; Extended Evolutionary Synthesis

name: SECI Model
extended_summary: Ikujiro Nonaka and Hirotaka Takeuchi's model describes knowledge creation as a continuous spiral through four conversion modes between tacit and explicit knowledge: Socialization (tacit to tacit through shared experience), Externalization (tacit to explicit through articulation), Combination (explicit to explicit through systematic combination), and Internalization (explicit to tacit through embodied practice). The framework grew from study of Japanese knowledge-creating companies and has become foundational in knowledge management theory, though it has been criticized for ambiguity about what counts as tacit knowledge and for cultural specificity to its Japanese origin context.
core_components: Socialization (tacit-to-tacit); Externalization (tacit-to-explicit); Combination (explicit-to-explicit); Internalization (explicit-to-tacit); Ba (shared context); Knowledge spiral
primary_use_case: Knowledge management strategy; organizational learning design; innovation management.
common_criticisms: Ambiguity in operationalizing tacit knowledge; cultural specificity to Japanese organizational context; conceptual conflation of Polanyi's original tacit knowledge concept with practitioner-friendly simplification; difficulty empirically validating the four-mode structure.
primary_sources: Nonaka, I. & Takeuchi, H. (1995). The Knowledge-Creating Company; Nonaka, I. (1994). 'A Dynamic Theory of Organizational Knowledge Creation', Organization Science
siblings: Tacit and Explicit Knowledge; Communities of Practice; Five Disciplines

name: Eightfold Path
extended_summary: The Eightfold Path is the fourth of Buddhism's Four Noble Truths and articulates the Buddhist way of cessation of suffering through eight integrated aspects of practice. Traditionally grouped into three trainings — wisdom (right view, right intention), ethical conduct (right speech, right action, right livelihood), and mental discipline (right effort, right mindfulness, right concentration) — the path is understood as simultaneous rather than sequential cultivation. The framework is foundational across Buddhist traditions though specific interpretations vary substantially between Theravada, Mahayana, and Vajrayana lineages.
core_components: Right view; Right intention; Right speech; Right action; Right livelihood; Right effort; Right mindfulness; Right concentration
primary_use_case: Foundational Buddhist practice across all major traditions; ethical and contemplative framework adapted in secular mindfulness contexts.
common_criticisms: Translation of 'right' (samma) is culturally loaded; secularized interpretations strip the framework from its Four Noble Truths context; tension between simultaneous cultivation and pedagogical sequencing; differences between traditional interpretations make 'the' Eightfold Path somewhat misleading.
primary_sources: Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta (the Buddha's first discourse); Magga-vibhanga Sutta (analysis of the path); compiled in the Pali Canon
siblings: Four Noble Truths; Three Marks of Existence; Eight Limbs of Yoga

name: Stoic Dichotomy of Control
extended_summary: The Stoic distinction, articulated most clearly by Epictetus in the opening of the Enchiridion, divides phenomena into what is up to us (our judgments, intentions, desires, aversions) and what is not up to us (our bodies, possessions, reputations, others' actions). The framework's practical implication is that wellbeing depends on directing concern toward the former category and accepting the latter with equanimity. Modern Stoic-inspired practice in psychology and self-development has popularized the dichotomy widely, though some contemporary Stoic scholarship distinguishes a more nuanced 'trichotomy' that includes things partially within our control.
year_or_decade: 1st-2nd century CE (Epictetus); 3rd century BCE founding of Stoicism (Zeno of Citium)
core_components: What is up to us (prohairesis, our faculty of choice and judgment); What is not up to us (externals); Equanimity toward the latter; Active engagement with the former
primary_use_case: Stoic practice; cognitive behavioral therapy traces some lineage here; modern self-development and resilience practices.
common_criticisms: Strict dichotomy may be too binary — Irvine and others propose a trichotomy including partial control; risk of fatalism if applied carelessly; modern popularization sometimes detaches the dichotomy from broader Stoic ethics.
primary_sources: Epictetus (c. 135 CE). Enchiridion; Epictetus. Discourses (compiled by Arrian)
siblings: Stoicism; Memento Mori; Negative Visualization; Wu Wei

name: Capability Approach
extended_summary: Amartya Sen's framework, substantially developed in collaboration with Martha Nussbaum, evaluates individual wellbeing and social arrangements by what people are actually able to do and be — their capabilities — rather than by resources, utility, or preference satisfaction. The approach distinguishes between functionings (achieved doings and beings) and capabilities (the freedom to achieve various functionings) and provides foundational philosophy for the UN Human Development Index. Nussbaum extends Sen's framework with a list of central capabilities she argues are universally required for human dignity, while Sen resists settling on a fixed list, treating the choice of capabilities as itself a democratic question.
core_components: Functionings (achieved doings and beings); Capabilities (freedoms to achieve functionings); Conversion factors (personal, social, environmental); Agency; Nussbaum's list of central capabilities (in her variant)
primary_use_case: Development economics and policy evaluation; foundation of the UN Human Development Index; philosophical basis for justice theory; product and service design centered on capability expansion.
common_criticisms: Operationalization for measurement is contested — which capabilities and how to weight them; tension between Sen's procedural openness and Nussbaum's substantive list; difficulty distinguishing capability from preference in practice; resource-intensive to measure compared to GDP-style indicators.
primary_sources: Sen, A. (1979). 'Equality of What?' (Tanner Lecture); Sen, A. (1999). Development as Freedom; Nussbaum, M. (2000). Women and Human Development
siblings: Veil of Ignorance; Utilitarianism; Care Ethics

name: Wu Wei
extended_summary: Wu wei (literally 'non-action' or 'effortless action') is a foundational Taoist concept describing action that is in harmony with the natural flow of things rather than forced against it. The framework appears in both the Tao Te Ching and the Zhuangzi and has been variously interpreted as non-interference, spontaneous responsiveness, skilled action that has become second nature, and political quietism. Western interpretations in psychology have linked wu wei to Csikszentmihalyi's flow state, while traditional Confucian and Taoist scholarship distinguishes more carefully between wu wei as moral cultivation and wu wei as cosmic principle.
originators: Lao Tzu (Tao Te Ching, traditional attribution); Zhuangzi (extension)
core_components: Acting without forcing; Alignment with the Tao (way); Spontaneity (ziran); Effortlessness in skilled action; Non-interference
primary_use_case: Taoist contemplative practice; Chinese philosophical and political thought; modern integration into psychology of flow and skilled performance.
common_criticisms: Often misread as passivity in Western contexts; political readings (especially Han Feizi's) appropriate it for ruler quietism in ways the original may not support; modern psychological flow analogies risk decontextualizing it from Taoist cosmology.
primary_sources: Lao Tzu (c. 4th century BCE). Tao Te Ching; Zhuangzi (4th-3rd century BCE). Zhuangzi
siblings: Tao Te Ching Framework; Stoic Dichotomy of Control; Flow Theory

name: Hero's Journey
extended_summary: Joseph Campbell's monomyth pattern abstracts a recurring narrative structure across world mythologies in which a hero ventures from the ordinary world into a region of supernatural wonder, encounters fabulous forces, wins a decisive victory, and returns transformed with the power to bestow boons. Campbell organized the pattern into seventeen stages grouped under three acts (Departure, Initiation, Return), drawing heavily on Jungian depth psychology and comparative mythology. The framework has been enormously influential in storytelling, screenwriting (especially through Christopher Vogler's adaptation), and personal-development discourse, while attracting scholarly criticism for selection bias in its sources and for imposing Western masculine narrative templates universally.
core_components: Departure (call to adventure, refusal, mentor, threshold crossing); Initiation (trials, abyss, transformation, atonement); Return (refusal of return, threshold, master of two worlds, freedom to live); seventeen detailed stages
primary_use_case: Comparative mythology; screenwriting and narrative craft; Jungian-influenced personal development; analysis of cultural narratives.
common_criticisms: Selection bias in source mythologies (particularly underweights non-narrative and non-quest traditions); imposes a Western masculine quest template universally; conflates structurally distinct traditions; some scholars argue the universality claim does not survive rigorous comparative analysis.
primary_sources: Campbell, J. (1949). The Hero with a Thousand Faces; Vogler, C. (1992). The Writer's Journey (popular adaptation)
siblings: Jungian Archetypes; Three-Act Structure; Save the Cat Beat Sheet; Story Circle

name: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
extended_summary: The NIST CSF provides a voluntary risk-based framework for organizations to manage cybersecurity, organized around six core functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) — Govern was added in version 2.0 released in 2024 — alongside categories, subcategories, and informative references mapping to specific controls in frameworks like NIST 800-53. The framework was originally developed under Executive Order 13636 to improve critical infrastructure cybersecurity and has been broadly adopted across critical infrastructure sectors and beyond, including international adoption. Implementation tiers and target/current state profiles allow organizations to articulate cybersecurity maturity and improvement roadmaps in a standardized vocabulary.
originators: National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)
core_components: Six core functions: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover; Categories and subcategories under each function; Implementation tiers (1-4); Profiles (current state and target state); Informative references mapping to control catalogs
primary_use_case: Cybersecurity risk management for critical infrastructure and other organizations; common vocabulary for cybersecurity maturity discussions; mapping organizational controls to standardized outcomes.
common_criticisms: Voluntary nature limits enforcement; outcome-focused approach can leave implementation ambiguity; substantial mapping work needed when organizations also follow ISO 27001 or other standards; subcategories number in the hundreds, creating coverage burden.
primary_sources: NIST (2014). Framework for Improving Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity v1.0; NIST (2024). Cybersecurity Framework v2.0
siblings: ISO/IEC 27001; CIS Controls; NIST 800-53; NIST Risk Management Framework

name: Basel III
extended_summary: Basel III is the third major iteration of the Basel Accords on bank capital and liquidity standards, developed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision in response to weaknesses revealed in the 2008 financial crisis. The framework substantially raises minimum capital requirements, introduces a leverage ratio backstop independent of risk weights, and introduces explicit liquidity standards (the Liquidity Coverage Ratio for short-term and the Net Stable Funding Ratio for structural). National regulators implement Basel III with local variations — the US implementation through the Federal Reserve, OCC, and FDIC has substantially different details than the EU's CRR/CRD implementation. Final post-2008 reforms, sometimes called Basel IV, are still phasing in across jurisdictions.
core_components: Common Equity Tier 1 minimum (4.5%) plus capital conservation buffer (2.5%); Total Tier 1 minimum (6%); Total capital minimum (8%); Leverage ratio (3% minimum); Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR); Net Stable Funding Ratio (NSFR); Countercyclical buffer; G-SIB surcharges
primary_use_case: Prudential regulation of banks worldwide; capital and liquidity adequacy assessment; basis for stress testing regimes like CCAR.
common_criticisms: Risk-weight calibration remains contested and model-dependent; complexity creates compliance burden disproportionately affecting smaller banks; cyclicality concerns about capital requirements amplifying downturns; arbitrage opportunities between banking and shadow banking sectors.
primary_sources: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2010-2017). Basel III: A global regulatory framework for more resilient banks and banking systems and subsequent revisions
siblings: CCAR; DFAST; CECL; CAMELS Rating

name: COSO ERM
extended_summary: COSO Enterprise Risk Management is the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations' framework for enterprise-level risk management, integrating strategy and performance with risk consideration. The 2017 revision (Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance) substantially restructured the earlier 2004 framework around five interrelated components and twenty principles, emphasizing risk's role in strategy formulation rather than treating it as compliance overlay. COSO ERM is widely adopted by US public companies and is referenced in audit and regulatory expectations even where not formally required.
originators: Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (COSO)
core_components: Five components: Governance & Culture; Strategy & Objective-Setting; Performance; Review & Revision; Information, Communication & Reporting; Twenty principles supporting the components
primary_use_case: Enterprise risk management programs at large organizations; reference framework for risk committees and audit functions; basis for regulatory expectations around risk management.
common_criticisms: Volume and complexity create implementation burden; principles can be applied superficially as documentation exercises; integration with strategy can be aspirational rather than operational; substantial overlap with COSO Internal Control framework creates confusion about which to apply when.
primary_sources: COSO (2004). Enterprise Risk Management — Integrated Framework; COSO (2017). Enterprise Risk Management — Integrating with Strategy and Performance
siblings: COSO Internal Control-Integrated Framework; ISO 31000; Three Lines Model; FAIR

name: ISO/IEC 27001
extended_summary: ISO/IEC 27001 specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually improving an information security management system (ISMS). The standard takes a risk-based approach centered on a Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle with management commitment, risk assessment and treatment, and a Statement of Applicability documenting which controls from Annex A (which references ISO 27002) are applied. Certification by accredited bodies allows organizations to demonstrate ISMS conformance, making 27001 a frequent contractual requirement particularly for cloud and managed service providers. The 2022 revision substantially restructured Annex A from fourteen control categories to four themes (organizational, people, physical, technological).
core_components: Context establishment; Leadership commitment; Risk assessment and treatment; Statement of Applicability; Annex A controls (referencing ISO 27002); PDCA cycle; Internal audit; Management review; Continual improvement
primary_use_case: Information security management system certification; demonstrating security maturity to customers and regulators; structured framework for security program design.
common_criticisms: Process-heavy approach can produce documentation without genuine security improvement; certification audits sample-based and time-bounded; substantial implementation cost particularly for small organizations; Annex A control set may not address all domain-specific risks.
primary_sources: ISO/IEC 27001:2022. Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection — Information security management systems — Requirements
siblings: ISO/IEC 27002; NIST Cybersecurity Framework; SOC 2; HITRUST CSF

name: GDPR
extended_summary: The General Data Protection Regulation is the European Union's comprehensive data protection law, applicable since May 2018, governing processing of personal data of EU residents. The regulation's substantial extraterritorial reach — applying to non-EU organizations that process EU residents' data — has made it a de facto global standard for many multinational organizations. GDPR is built around principles including lawfulness, purpose limitation, data minimization, and accountability, and grants data subjects rights including access, rectification, erasure, and portability. Enforcement is by national data protection authorities with fines up to 4% of global annual revenue, which has produced multi-hundred-million-euro penalties against major technology companies.
originators: European Parliament and Council of the European Union
core_components: Six lawful bases for processing; Seven data protection principles; Data subject rights (access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection, restriction, automated decision-making); Data Protection Impact Assessments; Data Protection Officer requirement (in specified cases); Data breach notification (72-hour); Cross-border transfer mechanisms
primary_use_case: Data protection compliance for organizations processing EU residents' personal data; foundation for many subsequent privacy regimes globally; basis for privacy-by-design and privacy engineering practices.
common_criticisms: Compliance burden disproportionate for small organizations; consent fatigue from cookie banners and notices; conflict with other regulatory regimes (particularly US national security data access); enforcement uneven across member states; tension with AI/ML training data requirements.
primary_sources: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 (GDPR), Official Journal of the European Union
siblings: CCPA; HIPAA; Privacy by Design; FIPPs
